questions.q: Define dramatic irony in your own words and give one example from *The Proposal*.
questions.a: Dramatic irony is when the audience knows something the characters do not. In *The Proposal*, the audience knows Lomov came to propose, but Lomov and Natalya argue about Oxen Meadows instead. A wrong answer (e.g., “It’s when something unexpected happens”) shows the student confuses dramatic irony with situational irony.

questions.q: Explain why the Oxen Meadows argument is an instance of dramatic irony. What does the audience know that the characters ignore?
questions.a: The audience knows Lomov’s visit is for a marriage proposal, but Lomov and Natalya forget this and fight over land ownership. The irony lies in the proposal being “lost” in the argument. A wrong answer that merely summarizes the argument without mentioning the audience’s superior knowledge reveals a lack of understanding of the “audience vs. character” knowledge gap.

questions.q: In the dog argument (Act 2), Lomov says, “My Guess is better than your Squeezer.” Identify the dramatic irony in this moment and explain its effect on the audience.
questions.a: Step 1: Recall Lomov’s original purpose — proposal. Step 2: Note that the dog argument erupts *after* the proposal is temporarily settled. Step 3: The audience knows the proposal is still not formally completed, yet the characters fight over dogs. Step 4: This prolongs the irony and heightens comic frustration. A wrong answer that only describes the dog fight misses the layering of irony (proposal forgotten twice).

questions.q: Compare the dramatic irony in the Oxen Meadows argument and the dog argument. Which one more sharply highlights the theme of absurdity? Justify.
questions.a: The Oxen Meadows argument is the first diversion; the dog argument is a second diversion *after* the proposal was almost made. The dog argument is more absurd because the characters have already agreed to marry but still fight over trivialities. A wrong answer that treats both arguments as identical fails to analyze the escalation of absurdity.

questions.q: Evaluate: Does Chekhov’s use of dramatic irony make the play funnier, or does it make the characters seem merely foolish? Support your view with evidence.
questions.a: It does both: the irony creates humour through the audience’s superior knowledge, but it also satirizes the characters’ foolishness — their pride and pettiness override a life-changing event. A balanced evaluation citing both effects (e.g., Chubukov’s “She’s willing!” vs. the renewed dog fight) shows deep engagement. A one-sided answer (“only funny” or “only foolish”) misses the satirical purpose.

questions.q: Write a 4‑line dialogue between two friends where dramatic irony is used: the audience knows a secret the speakers do not.
questions.a: A good answer creates a clear knowledge gap (e.g., Friend A: “I’m sure Riya will hate this gift.” Friend B: “She told me she loves surprises.” Audience knows Riya is allergic to the gift). A poor answer lacks a secret known only to the audience, showing the student hasn’t grasped the “audience vs. character” structure.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows crucial ______ that the characters on stage do not; in *The Proposal*, the audience knows Lomov has come to propose marriage, but Lomov, Natalya, and Chubukov get entangled in petty arguments over Oxen Meadows and dogs, completely sidelining the proposal.

Fill in the blank: Imagine watching a movie where you know the main character is about to walk into a ______ party, but the character thinks they’re walking into an empty house — you feel the tension and humour of that gap.
Fill in the blank: In *The Proposal*, start by recalling Lomov’s actual purpose (marriage proposal) from node ______.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify at least two specific instances of dramatic irony in the play, explain how each instance creates humour and underscores the theme of absurdity, and write a structured answer using the PEEL method (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) with accurate textual references.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine ______ a movie where you know the main character is about to walk into a surprise party, but the character thinks they’re walking into an empty house — you feel the tension and humour of that gap.
